terms.definition: How often a model is right on test examples it has never seen: the number right divided by the number tested, as a percentage.
A security app that looks for harmful programs, like viruses, and stops them.
A program you use for one job, like a game, a browser or a music player.
Your OK for an app to use something on your device, like the camera, microphone, location or contacts, which you can change later in Settings.
Software that learns patterns from lots of examples, instead of only following rules a person wrote, so it can make guesses about new things.
An app that shows a fresh sign-in code every 30 seconds or so, which you type after your password as a second proof it is really you.
The DNS server that's in charge of a domain name and holds its records, so it has the real answer.
A program running without a window, doing a job for you, like checking for updates or syncing files.
Copied somewhere else (like the cloud or another drive), so it isn't lost if the original is deleted or broken.
When a model works better for some people or situations than others, usually because of gaps in its training data.
Counting with only two digits, 0 and 1, which is how computers store everything.
The smallest piece of data: a single 0 or 1, like a switch that's off or on.
An account run by a program instead of a person, posting and replying automatically.
The app you use to visit websites.
One open page in your browser, so you can have several open at once and switch between them.
A mistake in a program's code that makes it go wrong.
A group of 8 bits, which can hold a number from 0 to 255, or roughly one letter of plain English text.
A place that keeps a copy of something you used recently, so it's quicker to get next time.
A website's digital ID card, checked when you connect with HTTPS, that proves the site really owns its name.
A trusted organisation that checks who owns a website's name and then issues its certificate.
The device or app that asks a server for something, like your browser.
Storage and services on a company's servers, which you reach over the internet.
A DNS record that says a name is an alias: look up this other name instead.
An instruction you type into a terminal, like ipconfig, then run by pressing Enter.
How much text a chatbot can look at at once, so in a very long chat the earliest messages can fall out of it and be forgotten.
One complete worker inside a CPU, so a CPU with 4 cores can work on 4 things at once.
The chip that follows a program's instructions: the device's brain.
Using the internet or phones to be mean to someone so they feel bad or upset: hurtful messages, posts, threats or leaving them out on purpose.
When information a company keeps, such as email addresses and passwords, is stolen or leaked.
A fake video or picture made with AI, showing a real person doing or saying something they never did.
The router a device sends data to when it's going outside its own network, which at home is your home router.
Everything about you that ends up online: what you post, what others post about you, and what apps and websites record.
The internet's phone book, which turns names like example.com into IP addresses.
A website's name, like example.com, which people use instead of the number computers use to find the site (its IP address).
Scrambling data with a secret key so that only the right people or devices can unscramble and read it.
To save a finished piece of work, like a video, as a file that other apps and people can use.
The end of a file's name after the last dot, like .jpg, which tells the computer what kind of file it is.
One named piece of saved data, like a photo, a song or an essay.
A container for files, and for other folders, like a box inside a box.
AI that makes new things, like text, pictures, music or voices, from patterns it learned in huge amounts of examples.
A billion ticks per second, the unit a CPU's clock speed is measured in.
A unit for amounts of data, equal to 1,000 megabytes, used for phone storage and RAM.
The system a phone uses to work out where it is (its location), using signals from satellites.
When an AI chatbot says something false, smoothly and confidently, because it picks words that sound likely rather than checking facts.
A few quick messages two devices swap to set up a connection before sending the real data.
The physical parts of a device that you could touch, like the screen, battery and chips.
An extra line of information at the start of a message, like which website a request is for.
Counting with 16 digits, 0 to 9 then A to F, where one hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits.
One step of a packet's journey: from your device to the first router, then from each router to the next.
The code that describes a web page: its headings, text, links and pictures.
The rules browsers and web servers use to ask for and send web pages.
HTTP sent inside an encrypted connection, so people in between can't read or change it.
When someone uses your personal details, like your name, birthday or address, to pretend to be you.
The protocol email apps usually use to read mail that's kept on your mail provider's server.
The number that works as a device's address on a network, so data can find it.
The original kind of IP address: 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255, like 192.168.1.20.
The newer, much bigger kind of IP address: 128 bits, written in hex groups, like 2001:db8::1.
The company that connects your home to the internet.
A model, trained on huge amounts of text, that predicts which word (token) is likely to come next, and that chatbots are built on.
A family of operating systems, like Windows but free to use, that runs many servers and some laptops.
The kind of rechargeable battery in phones and laptops, which holds a lot of energy for its size, so it must be treated with care.
A web address made to look like a real one: a letter swapped, an extra word added, or a different ending.
A setting that makes a device save energy, for example by pausing background apps, so the battery lasts longer.
A way of making AI: the computer is shown many examples and finds the patterns in them itself.
A unit for amounts of data, equal to 1,000 kilobytes or a million bytes, so a phone photo is a few MB.
A bug where an app keeps taking RAM and never gives it back, so it uses more and more over time.
A thousandth of a second.
False information that spreads, whether someone meant it or not, and that AI makes quicker and cheaper to make.
What a computer builds from its training data: its own way of guessing the answer for new things it has never seen.
The main circuit board that all a device's parts plug into and send signals through.
A DNS record that names the server that receives email for a domain.
How a home router lets many devices share one public address, by swapping addresses and keeping a table.
A group of devices connected so they can send data to each other, like everything on your home Wi-Fi.
A group of 8 bits, like each of the four numbers (0 to 255) in an IPv4 address.
The main software that runs a device: it shares out the CPU and RAM, runs apps and looks after files.
When a model memorises its training examples, quirks and all, instead of the real pattern, so it does much worse on new examples.
A small piece of data sent across a network, with addresses added so it can find its way.
A way to sign in without a password, where your device proves it's you with your fingerprint, face or PIN, so a fake website can't steal it.
A password made of four or more random words, long enough to be hard to guess but easy for you to remember.
An app that creates, saves and fills in a different strong password for each account, so you only remember one main password.
The route through folders to a file, like Documents > School > essay.docx, or the part of a web address after the name.
Something that shows up again and again, like apples being round, which AI learns by finding in examples.
The actual data a packet carries, apart from the addresses and other added information.
A scam message, like an email, text or call, that pretends to be someone you trust to trick you into sharing details or clicking a link.
A number that picks which program on a computer a packet is for, like an apartment number in a building.
A model's best guess, based on the patterns it learned, which can be wrong even when it sounds sure.
An IP address for use inside a home, school or office network, where the same addresses are reused in millions of networks.
A program that's running right now, as listed in the task manager.
What you type (or say) to an AI tool like a chatbot or image maker, and a good one says the goal, who it's for, and the length or shape you want.
A set of rules that devices agree to follow so they can understand each other.
An IP address that's unique across the whole internet, so anyone on the internet can reach it.
Wi-Fi that anyone nearby can join, like at a café, library or airport.
The fast workspace for what's in use right now, which is cleared when the power goes off.
The DNS server that looks up a name for your device, asking other DNS servers if it doesn't already know.
One of the DNS servers at the top of the system, which know who handles each ending, like .com or .org.
A device that passes data between networks, choosing the next step each time, like the home router that links your home to the internet.
A router's list of where to send packets next, depending on their destination address.
A trick to get your money, personal details or passwords.
A weak spot in software that an attacker could use to get in, which updates fix.
An old, weak way to check it's you, like "What was your first pet's name?", because the answers can often be guessed or found online.
A number that marks where a piece of data belongs, so the pieces can be put back in order.
A computer that provides something, like a website, email or files, to other devices over a network.
When electricity takes a wrong shortcut between two contacts, which can damage a device or make it dangerously hot.
The protocol used to send email, from your app to your mail server and between mail servers.
A protocol for safely controlling another computer from far away.
An app set to open by itself as soon as the device switches on.
The number a web server sends back to say how a request went, like 200 (OK) or 404 (not found).
The part that keeps apps, photos and files, even when the power is off.
An extra part added on the left of a domain name by its owner, like www in www.example.com.
A setting (not a device's address) that says how big the local network is, meaning which addresses count as nearby.
A device that joins devices inside one network and passes data between them.
To keep two copies matched up, so a change on one (like your phone) also appears on the other (like the cloud).
A process that's part of the operating system itself, so ending one can crash or restart the device.
A tool in the operating system that lists every running process and lets you end one.
A protocol that makes sure data arrives complete and in order, resending anything that gets lost.
A setting that changes how a language model picks: low makes it predictable, high makes it more surprising (and more likely to make no sense).
A window where you control a computer by typing commands instead of tapping or clicking.
When a CPU slows itself down because it's too hot, to protect itself.
The last part of a domain name, like com in example.com, or uk in example.co.uk.
The protocol that encrypts HTTPS connections and checks the server's certificate.
A piece of text a language model works with: often a whole word, sometimes part of a long or unusual one.
A tool that lists the routers (hops) your packets pass through on the way to a destination.
The examples a model learns from, usually each with a label saying what it really is.
Signing in with your password plus a second proof, like an app code or your fingerprint, also called two-factor or multi-factor authentication (MFA).
A quick protocol that sends data without checking it arrived, good for live video and games, where speed matters most.
A new version of software that fixes bugs and security holes, and sometimes adds features.
A full web address, like https://www.example.com/news, saying which protocol, which site and which page.
A harmful program that spreads to other files or devices, which security apps look for.
A fake copy of someone's voice made with AI, which can say things the real person never said.
The maker's promise to repair a device for free if it breaks by itself within a set time.
A visible or hidden mark showing something was made by AI, which can be removed, so a missing one proves nothing.
A unit for how fast energy is used: a phone uses a few watts, and the more watts, the faster the battery empties.
The part of a network that sends out the Wi-Fi signal, so wireless devices can join.
